To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the presented method is an easy and efficient approach to the synthesis of well-defined sugar-modified polymethacrylates and that the obtained glycopolymeric materials are biocompatible and support cell adhesion.

a novel, efficient, and metal-catalysis free method was used to graft 1-thio-glucopyranoside and 1-thiol-galactopyranoide onto a PFS-based copolymers and the prepared polymers were cytocompatible with 3T3 and MC3T1-E1 cells and were used to prepare biocompatible coatings for culturing these cells.

the thiol/fluorine "click"-based glycopolymerization method is efficient, metal-catalyst-free and provides access to biocompatible glycopolymer films that can be used as coatings for biomedical devices.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis of a novel family of biocompatible and biodegradable polymers that may find applications as coatings in tissue engineering.
the synthesis of novel, biologically active, and water-insoluble glycopolymeric materials that may be used for the development of new biomaterials for tissue engineering applications.
an efficient and versatile method of preparing well-defined sugar-modified polymes that are suitable for biomedical applications, e.g., as synthetic coatings for cell adhesion and proliferation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the glycopolymeric coatings are biocompatible and promote cell adhesion.
the prepared glycopolymer coatings are biocompatible for fibroblasts, preosteoblast and human umbilical vein endothelial cells.
the prepared glycopolymer films are biocompatible and can be used as coatings for biomedical implants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed an efficient method of glycopolymers synthesis via thiol-fluorine reaction, and the resulting polymers were not toxic to cells and supported cell adhesion and proliferation.
the glycopolymeric surfaces were found to be suitable for cell adhesion and proliferation.
the PFS-based glycopolymer films are promising candidates for biomedical coatings.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PFS backbone can be used to prepare well-defined, biocompatible glycopolymeric materials with a potential for biomedical applications.
the PFS-based polymers can be used as a versatile scaffold for cell growth, and that the incorporation of carbohydrates into these scaffolds can be used to modulate cell adhesion.
the glycosylated polymeric films are biocompatible and that the cell adhesion is influenced by the carbohydrate composition.
